## Choose the System Before Counting {#sec-lay-ch02}

## A Concrete Picture

Picture a household checking its finances. A payment to a spouse leaves one
person's wallet but stays inside the household. The money has crossed one
boundary, not the other. A mechanical energy account also needs an inventory
of what is inside. The club, the hands and club, and the entire golfer and club
are different systems, even when we observe the same swing.

There is one crucial limit to the analogy: a force is not an energy payment.
A golfer can push against a stationary surface and change whole-body momentum
while the contact does no mechanical work. Muscles can convert chemical energy,
and tissues can release stored energy, while the ground supplies the reaction
that makes the motion possible. The reaction matters without being the energy
source. A deforming surface or moving support requires a different account.

Before saying that the arms, wrists, shaft or ground supplied energy, ask which
bodies and interface elements are included, which observer measures velocity,
and which forms of energy are being counted. Those choices make a claim
testable. They also explain why a force, a negative moment and a positive
energy transfer are three different observations.

![The Chosen Body Inventory Determines Which Interactions Cross the Boundary.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_system_boundaries.svg){#fig-lay-system-boundaries width=96% fig-alt="Three system inventories distinguish the club, golfer and club, and golfer, club and Earth. Hand contact, ground contact and gravity change their boundary classification; an interaction label alone does not establish positive work."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Draw the Boundary Through Named Bodies

For the **club alone**, include the head, shaft and grip material. The hands,
air and ball can apply external loads. Earth's gravity is also an external
force. A flexible shaft stores strain energy and has moving mass; its energy
is not just a massless spring's storage. Grip or contact compliance belongs
where the model explicitly places it, rather than disappearing between two
subsystem drawings.

Expanding the inventory changes the ports at which loads and motion must be
paired. Here, a *port* means an identified interface across which mechanical
power is evaluated, not an additional energy source.

| Included Bodies | Interfaces That Still Cross the Boundary |
|:--|:--|
| Head, shaft and grip | Hand contact, air and ball contact; gravity remains an external force |
| Both hands and the club | Wrist interfaces with the forearms; grip contact is internal |
| Both upper arms, forearms, hands and club | Shoulder interfaces with the torso; elbows and wrists are internal |
| The golfer's body and club | Foot-ground, air and ball interfaces; gravity remains external unless Earth is included |

These are model inventories, not sharp anatomical compartments. A muscle or
tendon spanning an interface needs an explicit allocation. For the golfer-club
mechanical account, muscle actuation converts energy within the included
biological system. It can increase mechanical energy without external work.
If chemical and thermal energy are also tracked, conversion and dissipation
move energy between forms instead of creating or destroying total energy.

Adding Earth internalizes the golfer-ground interaction and the mutual
gravitational interaction. It does not automatically include the air, ball,
Sun or every environmental interaction, and does not by itself make the
enlarged system isolated. Keep the actual inventory, not merely the phrase
“whole system,” beside the balance.

### Ground Reaction Is Not Ground Work

For an applied contact force, the instantaneous power delivered to the chosen
body is

$$
P_{\mathrm{contact}}=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_{\mathrm{contact}}.
$$

The velocity is that of the body's material point where the force acts, in the
declared observer frame. A contact moment adds its power-conjugate angular
term. For distributed contact, sum or integrate the local load-velocity
pairings. A stationary, ideal sticking contact has zero local velocity and
zero force power; a stationary support that also prevents rotation has zero
contact-moment power. These are kinematic assumptions, not universal properties
of shoes, turf or force plates [@widnall2008work].

For a fixed-mass system in an inertial frame, Newton's equation also gives

$$
\frac{dK_G}{dt}=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot\mathbf v_G,
\qquad K_G=\tfrac12 M\lVert\mathbf v_G\rVert^2,
$$

where $G$ is the system center of mass and $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the
resultant external force. This is a balance for **COM translational kinetic
energy**, sometimes called a pseudowork relation. The actual application
points need not move with $G$. Consequently, its right-hand side is not
generally the external mechanical power of an extended or deforming system.

Consider a deliberately simple manufactured example, with gravity omitted.
Two masses of $2$ kg are connected by an internal actuator. The lower mass
stays against a stationary unilateral support. An actuator force of $40$ N
pushes the upper mass through $0.5$ m from rest and pushes the lower mass into
the support. The support supplies $40$ N in the opposite direction but its
point moves zero distance, so its work is zero. The actuator converts $20$ J
into motion. The upper mass reaches $\sqrt{20}$ m/s, giving $20$ J total
kinetic energy, of which $10$ J is COM kinetic energy and $10$ J is motion
relative to the COM. An ideal internal energy reservoir falls by $20$ J.

The COM moves $0.25$ m: support force times COM displacement is $10$ J,
consistent with the COM equation, but it is not $10$ J supplied by the support.
Removing the support produces a different problem: the two initially resting
free masses move apart while their combined momentum remains zero. This is
why internal actuation, external reaction and energy transfer must be kept
together without identifying them with one another. The example illustrates
accounting; it is not a quantitative model of a golfer's push-off.

### Internal Contact Power Cancels Only Under the Right Conditions

Let body 1 receive contact force $\mathbf F$ and contact moment $\mathbf M$,
and body 2 receive their opposites at the same contact location. Express all
vectors in common axes. Their combined mechanical power is

$$
P_1+P_2=\mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2)
+\mathbf M\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega_1-\boldsymbol\omega_2).
$$

Equal and opposite loads cancel in a force or moment sum; power also needs the
local motions. Coincident spatial contact positions need not have equal
material-point velocities during slip. Compatible motion in an ideal passive
constraint makes the load-relative-motion pairing zero. Equality of every
velocity component is sufficient but not necessary: a force perpendicular to
relative motion also contributes zero power.

For example, with force on body 1 equal to $(-4,0,10)$ N and contact velocities
$(5,1,0)$ and $(2,1,0)$ m/s, the two force powers are $-20$ W and $+8$ W.
Their sum is $-12$ W. This is consistent with sliding friction opposing the
relative tangential motion; the normal component does no work here. The
mechanical loss needs a thermal or other nonrecoverable-energy account. The
power calculation alone does not identify how that loss is distributed.

A compliant interface can also store energy. For an explicitly massless,
passive interface with storage $U_c$ and nonnegative dissipation $D_c$, its
powers on the adjoining bodies satisfy $P_1+P_2=-\dot U_c-D_c$. Include
interface kinetic energy if it has inertia, and an actuator conversion term
if it is powered. A joint actuator's torque pairs with **relative** angular
velocity when computing its combined mechanical contribution; a torque's
power on one segment is a different quantity.

Two skaters pushing apart therefore do not establish that their mutual contact
must supply positive external work to each skater. Internal deformation and
chemical conversion can raise their kinetic energies even with a stationary
common contact. For the golfer, draw separate arm-side, club-side and interface
accounts before assigning an energy source. Constraint reaction, transmission,
storage, actuation and loss can all participate in the same motion.

### Count Gravity Once

Gravity can remain an external force for a club-only body inventory while its
prescribed, time-independent field is represented by an effective potential.
For uniform downward gravity, let $U_g=\sum_i m_i g z_i$; then

$$
P_g=-\dot U_g.
$$

Earth need not have simulated degrees of freedom inside the body inventory
for this representation to be useful. Distinguish that effective external-field
potential from the mutual interaction energy of a dynamical Earth-club model.
With $U_e$ denoting included elastic storage, two equivalent mechanical
accounts are

$$
\frac{d(K+U_e)}{dt}=P_g+P_{\mathrm{other}}+P_{\mathrm{act}}-D,
$$

$$
\frac{d(K+U_e+U_g)}{dt}=P_{\mathrm{other}}+P_{\mathrm{act}}-D.
$$

Here $P_{\mathrm{other}}$ is external mechanical power excluding gravity,
$P_{\mathrm{act}}$ is included actuation's mechanical conversion, and $D$ is
the modeled loss from recoverable mechanical energy. Do not put $U_g$ on the
left while also counting $P_g$ on the right. A falling body makes the error
obvious: its kinetic increase balances its potential decrease without a second
gravitational deposit. A time-dependent field needs the additional explicit
time-dependence term; the displayed equivalence assumes a static potential.

For an unpowered club-only inventory, $P_{\mathrm{act}}=0$: the golfer's work
already enters through the hand-contact port. Adding wrist-actuator work again
would count the same input twice under that boundary.

The zero of potential may be shifted by a fixed constant without changing
these balances. That freedom does not change the body inventory or permit
dropping a changing energy term.

Earth's recoil requires an equally explicit frame. If a constant mass $M_E$
has initial COM velocity $\mathbf V$ and receives total impulse $\mathbf J$,
its translational kinetic change in that inertial frame is

$$
\Delta K_E=\mathbf V\cdot\mathbf J+
\frac{\lVert\mathbf J\rVert^2}{2M_E}.
$$

For bounded impulse and an initially resting receiver, large mass makes the
quadratic recoil small. It does not eliminate the first term in another
observer's account. Rotation, local ground deformation and slip are separate
quantities; negligible COM recoil does not prove zero foot-ground work. For a
short golf-swing calculation, state the laboratory-frame approximation and
support assumptions rather than relying on mass alone.

### Change a Reporting Point Without Changing the Observer

For a rigid body, resultant force $\mathbf R$, moment about $A$ and the rigid
velocity field give total wrench power

$$
P=\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf v_A+\mathbf M_A\cdot\boldsymbol\omega.
$$

Moving the reporting point to $B$ requires both transformations:

$$
\mathbf M_B=\mathbf M_A-(\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A)\times\mathbf R,
\qquad
\mathbf v_B=\mathbf v_A+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A).
$$

The two extra scalar-triple-product terms cancel in power. Consistently
rotating the component axes also preserves the scalar. These operations
represent the **same physical motion for the same observer**; $\mathbf v_B$
is the rigid velocity field evaluated at $B$, not an unrelated anatomical
point's velocity [@lynchParkWrenches]. Only a pure couple, with zero resultant,
has a moment independent of reporting point.

Changing to a nonrotating inertial observer moving at constant velocity
$\mathbf U$ instead changes every material-point velocity by $-\mathbf U$.
For the same Newtonian applied loads,

$$
P'=P-\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf U.
$$

Work and kinetic energy change together; the work-energy equation retains its
form, but those quantities need not have the same numerical values
[@diaz2009frames]. A zero-resultant couple has no boost term. Neither operation
changes the physical swing. A reader comparing two reports must first align
the body inventory, observer, moment point, signs and interval.

### What a Net Club Wrench Can Hide

For a rigid club, the same complete applied-wrench history, inertial
parameters, other loads and initial state give the same trajectory under the
same well-posed dynamics. That does not identify how the two hands or the
muscles produced those loads. Opposing hand forces can partly cancel in the
resultant while generating a couple; an opposing pair along the line joining
the contacts can also have zero resultant moment. The latter can change grip
loading without appearing in the net wrench.

Flexibility adds another limitation. At positions $(-1,0,0)$ and $(1,0,0)$ m,
apply outward axial forces $(-1,0,0)$ and $(1,0,0)$ N. The resultant force and
moment are both zero. If the material points move outward at $1$ m/s each,
the loads nevertheless supply $2$ W of deformation power. Zero loads give the
same resultant wrench but zero power. For one rigid velocity field, that
self-equilibrated pair would give zero power instead. A net-wrench measurement
therefore does not determine all flexible-body power, deformation or internal
load allocation. This manufactured contrast establishes a possibility, not
its magnitude in a human grip.

These distinctions connect the later two-hand and shaft chapters. A negative
projected couple is not automatically negative total power. Positive hand
power is not automatically the power of a particular muscle. Shaft energy
release is not automatically an equal increase in clubhead energy: handle
exchange, shaft kinetic energy and dissipation also enter. Different boundary
accounts are useful because they expose these simultaneous pathways.

### Audit the Ledger Before Explaining the Swing

Suppose the club gains $40$ J while an arm loses $12$ J. Those endpoint changes
do not establish that the arm supplied exactly $12$ J to the club. Integrate
the appropriate interface powers and account for actuation, gravity, storage,
other segment exchanges and losses over the same interval. A closed total
energy account still does not reveal a unique anatomical pathway.

**Model Result:** The pinned technical treatment separates two-sided
interface power, elastic storage and whole-system residuals. It also records
differences between reconstructed and archived power columns. Algebraic closure
or solver convergence verifies a declared calculation; it does not independently
validate anatomy, contact laws or angular-momentum closure. Each balance needs
its own check.

**Human Evidence:** Nesbit and Serrano's four-subject analysis combines measured
kinematics with full-body and flexible-club models. Its compliant ground-contact
model differs from the stationary-support example above. Comparing modeled
vertical ground reactions with force-plate data does not directly measure all
joint loads or individual muscle work [@nesbit2005work]. Net joint power remains
a model-dependent quantity, with anatomical allocation requiring additional
evidence [@winter2009].

**Hypothesis:** Simultaneous handle, shaft and segment accounts may reveal a
transfer pathway that segment-speed plots miss. Testing it requires compatible
measurements or model states, explicit interface storage, matched intervals
and a declared endpoint; agreement with one energy ledger is insufficient.

**Practical Interpretation:** Write down the included bodies, observer and
stored forms. Locate each load's material-point motion, count gravity once,
then check subsystem and total balances. Only then ask which mechanism the
evidence identifies and which competing allocations remain possible.

## Where the Picture Breaks

Unlike a household payment, a segment-energy change need not have a unique
anatomical payer. Coordinate choices redistribute inertial terms; muscles can
span joints; soft tissue and contact layers store and dissipate energy. A
modeled wrist can aggregate carpal motion, forearm rotation, grip deformation
and translation. A modeled shoulder can aggregate several anatomical motions.
The body inventory and power convention remain useful only when those
approximations are explicit.

Equal energy does not imply equal tissue loading, comfort, accuracy, control
effort or repeatability. Energy accounting supplies consistency constraints
and exposes possible pathways. Those other outcomes need their own quantities
and evidence. The goal is a connected explanation of the swing, with each
ledger answering its own question without claiming to answer all of them.

develops the rigid and flexible accounts. Its

separates reference transport, allocation and contact-deformation power.
The manufactured examples here check mechanics identities; they do not
reproduce those archived simulations or validate a human intervention.
